lead.t: While Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) is generally the preferred first-line modality for both diagnosis and therapeutic intervention, it is not always technically feasible or successful.
lead.s: PTC and Percutaneous Biliary Drainage in Obstructive Jaundice

qs.q: A 56-year-old man with a complex Bismuth-Corlette type IV hilar cholangiocarcinoma is evaluated for biliary decompression. Which anatomical feature or clinical presentation makes percutaneous transhepatic cholangiography preferred over endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography in this patient?
o: A. Distal common bile duct choledocholithiasis
B. Presence of massive intractable ascites
C. Normal upper gastrointestinal anatomy
D. High biliary obstruction from complex lesions
qs.e: High hilar lesions such as Bismuth-Corlette type III or IV cholangiocarcinomas make selective cannulation of intrahepatic ducts via ERCP very challenging. Choledocholithiasis is typically treated with first-line ERCP rather than percutaneous approaches.
qs.s: PTC and Percutaneous Biliary Drainage in Obstructive Jaundice: MCQs

qs.q: A 62-year-old woman with a history of Roux-en-Y gastric bypass presents with obstructive jaundice due to a pancreatic head mass. Why is endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography typically not feasible in this patient?
o: A. Coagulopathy preventing scope passage through strictures
B. Prohibitive risk of pancreatitis and duodenal perforation
C. Anatomical alterations preventing access to ampulla
D. Massive ascites obstructing trans-oral endoscopic route
qs.e: Altered gastrointestinal anatomies such as Roux-en-Y gastric bypass prevent endoscopic access to the ampulla of Vater, necessitating percutaneous approaches. Ascites is a contraindication for percutaneous drainage rather than ERCP access.
qs.s: PTC and Percutaneous Biliary Drainage in Obstructive Jaundice: MCQs

qs.q: When comparing endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography and percutaneous transhepatic cholangiography/percutaneous biliary drainage, which of the following characteristics correctly distinguishes the percutaneous approach?
o: It is primarily performed via a trans-oral retrobulbar endoscopic route
It carries a primary risk of post-procedural acute clinical pancreatitis
It relies on transhepatic access under local anesthesia and moderate sedation
It is the preferred first-line modality for uncomplicated choledocholithiasis
qs.e: PTC/PBD uses a percutaneous transhepatic route under local anesthesia with moderate sedation, unlike ERCP which is trans-oral. ERCP remains the preferred first-line modality for choledocholithiasis and carries a risk of pancreatitis.
qs.s: PTC and Percutaneous Biliary Drainage in Obstructive Jaundice: MCQs

qs.q: A 50-year-old man is evaluated for biliary decompression. The medical team considers whether to perform endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography or a percutaneous transhepatic route. Which factor most strongly favors selecting the percutaneous approach?
o: High-grade hilar obstruction unsuitable for endoscopic access
Active acute pancreatitis following previous diagnostic instrumentation
Uncorrectable severe coagulopathy with marked thrombocytopenia
Massive refractory ascites needing frequent large-volume paracentesis
qs.e: High hilar obstructions are technically challenging for endoscopic access, making the percutaneous approach more favorable. Coagulopathy and massive ascites are major relative contraindications for percutaneous biliary drainage.
qs.s: PTC and Percutaneous Biliary Drainage in Obstructive Jaundice: MCQs

qs.q: A 52-year-old man with obstructive jaundice is evaluated to determine whether endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography or percutaneous transhepatic cholangiography is more appropriate. Which scenario typically necessitates the percutaneous approach?
o: Mildly raised serum bilirubin with normal liver synthetic function
Distal common bile duct stone readily accessible by standard endoscopy
Altered upper GI anatomy due to previous Roux‑en‑Y gastric bypass
Severe uncorrected thrombocytopenia with platelets under 20,000/µL
qs.e: Altered anatomy such as a Roux-en-Y gastric bypass prevents standard endoscopic retrograde access, making percutaneous transhepatic cholangiography necessary. Severe thrombocytopenia is a contraindication to the percutaneous approach, not an indication.
qs.s: PTC and Percutaneous Biliary Drainage in Obstructive Jaundice: MCQs
